$comment: The closed vocabulary of the fashion domain. Each fibre, fabric, material and finish gives its origin: the first year with a firm record, the place and, where known, the maker. circa = true marks an estimate. A null origin means that no open source gives a year. Fabrics have family 'textile'.

branches.name: Costume
branches.scope: The garments of day and evening dress: suits, coats, dresses, gowns, skirts, shirts, blouses, trousers and knitwear.

branches.name: Outdoor
branches.scope: Dress for weather, work, sport and the country: shell jackets, parkas, field and waxed jackets, trench coats, down and fleece.

branches.name: Underwear
branches.scope: Foundation and intimate garments under the dress: stays, corsets, brassieres, girdles, briefs, slips and stockings.

branches.name: Shoes
branches.scope: Footwear: dress shoes, boots, court shoes, sandals and sneakers, with their lasts, soles and heels.

branches.name: Accessories
branches.scope: Bags, luggage, hats, eyewear, neckwear, scarves, gloves and belts.

branches.name: Jewellery
branches.scope: Rings, necklaces, brooches, earrings, bracelets, tiaras and cufflinks, in metal, gems, pearls, enamel and paste.

branches.name: Watches
branches.scope: Pocket watches and wristwatches: the case, the dial, the hands, the crystal, the strap and the bracelet.

branches.name: Cars
branches.scope: The car as a fashion object: the body line, the paint, the brightwork, and the trim and upholstery of the cabin.

fibres.name: Flax (linen)
fibres.note: Linen cloth from flax is in Egyptian graves of about 5000 BC; dyed wild flax fibres from a cave in Georgia are about 30,000 years old.

fibres.name: Hemp
fibres.note: Hemp cloth is in Chinese graves of the third millennium BC; Europe used it for sailcloth, rope and work clothes.

fibres.name: Cotton
fibres.note: Cotton threads at Mehrgarh and cloth at Mohenjo-daro; Peru grew a second species from about 4500 BC.

fibres.name: Wool
fibres.note: Sheep with a woolly fleece appear in Mesopotamia in the fourth millennium BC; before that, sheep had hair.

fibres.name: Merino wool
fibres.note: Spain bred the fine merino sheep from about the 14th century and banned its export until the 18th century.

fibres.name: Silk
fibres.note: China reeled silk from the cocoon of Bombyx mori; Byzantium got silkworms in about AD 552.

fibres.name: Cashmere
fibres.note: The down of the Changthangi goat, woven into Kashmir shawls; Europe took the shawl as fashion from about 1800.

fibres.name: Mohair
fibres.note: The hair of the Angora goat; it gives a lustrous, springy yarn for suiting and knitwear.

fibres.name: Alpaca and vicuña
fibres.note: Andean weavers used alpaca and vicuña fibre in the Paracas textiles; vicuña is the finest animal fibre in commercial use.

fibres.name: Viscose rayon

origin.by: Charles Cross, Edward Bevan and Clayton Beadle

fibres.note: The first regenerated cellulose fibre made at scale; Chardonnet showed a nitrocellulose 'artificial silk' in 1889.

fibres.name: Cellulose acetate
fibres.note: A cellulose fibre with a silk-like drape and lustre, used for linings and evening dress.

fibres.name: Nylon
fibres.note: The first fully synthetic fibre; nylon stockings went on sale in 1940, and the war took the fibre for parachutes.

fibres.name: Polyester
fibres.note: A synthetic fibre that holds a crease and a pleat; it became the fibre of easy-care dress in the 1950s and 1960s.

fibres.name: Acrylic
fibres.note: A synthetic fibre with a wool-like hand, used for knitwear and fleece.

fibres.name: Elastane
fibres.note: A polyurethane fibre that stretches to five or more times its length and recovers; it replaced rubber thread in foundation garments.

fibres.name: Polypropylene
fibres.note: A light fibre that takes up almost no water; it became the first synthetic base layer in the 1970s.

fibres.name: Aramid
fibres.note: A heat- and cut-resistant fibre with high strength, used for protective clothing and racing suits.

fibres.name: Lyocell
fibres.note: A cellulose fibre spun from a solvent that the process recovers; it was sold from 1992.

fibres.name: Ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene
fibres.note: A gel-spun fibre with a high strength for its weight, used in light technical packs and shells.

fabrics.name: Linen cloth
fabrics.note: The oldest cloth of dress; cool, crisp and quick to crease. Shirts, summer suits and underwear were linen until cotton took over.

fabrics.name: Muslin
fabrics.note: A fine, open cotton of hand-spun yarn from Dhaka; the name comes from Mosul. It was the cloth of the Empire-line dress after 1795.

fabrics.name: Calico
fabrics.note: A plain cotton from the Malabar coast; England banned printed calico imports in 1700 and 1721 to protect wool and silk weavers.

fabrics.name: Glazed chintz
fabrics.note: A printed or painted cotton with a glazed surface; the East India companies brought it to Europe in the 17th century.

fabrics.name: Cambric (batiste)
fabrics.note: A fine, dense plain weave for shirts, collars, handkerchiefs and lingerie, named after the town of Cambrai.

fabrics.name: Poplin
fabrics.note: A plain weave with a fine weft rib; the name may come from 'papeline', the cloth of the papal town of Avignon. The cloth of the dress shirt.

fabrics.name: Oxford cloth
fabrics.note: A basket weave with a soft hand; Scottish mills named shirtings after universities. The cloth of the button-down shirt.

fabrics.name: Gingham
fabrics.note: A yarn-dyed check in white and one colour; the name comes from a Malay word for striped cloth.

fabrics.name: Seersucker
fabrics.note: Two warps at different tension make puckered stripes that stand off the skin; the name comes from Persian 'milk and sugar'.

fabrics.name: Canvas and duck
fabrics.note: A heavy plain weave for sails, tents, work coats and the upper of the first sneakers.

fabrics.name: Taffeta
fabrics.note: A crisp plain silk that rustles and holds a full skirt; the name comes from Persian 'taftah', twisted.

fabrics.name: Chiffon
fabrics.note: A sheer, floating plain weave of highly twisted yarn for overlays, scarves and evening dress.

fabrics.name: Crêpe de Chine
fabrics.note: A light silk with a pebbled surface from crepe-twisted weft; it drapes well on the bias.

fabrics.name: Denim
fabrics.note: A warp-faced twill with an indigo warp and a white weft; 'serge de Nîmes'. Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented the riveted work trouser in 1873.

fabrics.name: Serge
fabrics.note: A balanced twill with a clear diagonal rib, for uniforms, suits and coats.

fabrics.name: Gabardine
fabrics.note: A steep, tight twill of yarn proofed before the weave; it keeps out rain and lets the body breathe. The cloth of the trench coat.

fabrics.name: Tweed
fabrics.note: A rough, thick twill of woollen yarn; the name comes from 'tweel', misread by a London merchant as the River Tweed.

fabrics.name: Harris Tweed

origin.by: Lady Catherine Murray, Countess of Dunmore

fabrics.note: Hand-woven at home in the Outer Hebrides; the Orb mark dates from 1909 and an Act of Parliament protects the name since 1993.

fabrics.name: Worsted suiting
fabrics.note: A smooth, firm cloth of combed long-staple yarn, named after the Norfolk village; the cloth of the tailored suit.

fabrics.name: Flannel
fabrics.note: A soft cloth that is napped after the weave; grey wool flannel became the suit and trouser cloth of the 20th century.

fabrics.name: Khaki drill
fabrics.note: A cotton twill dyed the colour of dust ('khaki' in Urdu) for the Corps of Guides; armies took it for field dress.

fabrics.name: Chino twill
fabrics.note: A light cotton twill of US army trousers in the Philippines; the name comes from the Chinese cloth. It went to the campus after 1945.

fabrics.name: Tartan
fabrics.note: A twill check of coloured stripes in warp and weft; a check fragment from near Falkirk dates from about AD 250. The Dress Act of 1746 banned it in the Highlands.

fabrics.name: Houndstooth
fabrics.note: A broken check from a 2/2 twill with four dark and four light yarns in warp and weft.

fabrics.name: Satin
fabrics.note: A weave with long floats that gives a smooth, lustrous face; the name may come from Zaitun, the port of export.

fabrics.name: Silk twill
fabrics.note: A fine, dense silk twill that takes a sharp print; it is the cloth of the printed square scarf and the necktie. Twill silk is in Chinese graves of the second century BC.

fabrics.name: Damask
fabrics.note: A reversible figured cloth in which the pattern shows in satin on a ground of the opposite face; named after Damascus.

fabrics.name: Brocade
fabrics.note: A figured cloth with extra weft, often of metal thread, that floats on the face as a raised pattern; the cloth of court dress.

fabrics.name: Jacquard figured cloth
fabrics.note: Cloth from a loom that lifts each warp thread by a punched card; the cards made large figured patterns cheap.

fabrics.name: Velvet
fabrics.note: A warp-pile cloth with a short dense pile cut from a second warp; Italian cities wove it for courts and the church.

fabrics.name: Corduroy
fabrics.note: A weft-pile cloth with cut cords ('wales'); the cloth of country trousers and the 1970s jacket.

fabrics.name: Terry towelling
fabrics.note: A loop-pile cloth that Henry Christy saw in Turkey and his mill made by machine; the cloth of robes and sweatbands.

fabrics.name: Jersey
fabrics.note: A plain weft knit from the island knitters; Gabrielle Chanel made wool jersey into women's dress in 1916.

fabrics.name: Frame-knit hosiery
fabrics.note: Stockings from the knitting frame, the first textile machine of the modern kind; Nottingham became the centre of hosiery.

fabrics.name: Fair Isle knit
fabrics.note: A stranded knit in two colours each row; the Prince of Wales wore a Fair Isle jumper to golf in 1921.

fabrics.name: Aran knit
fabrics.note: A thick cream knit of cables, diamonds and moss stitch; it became a fashion knit in the 1950s.

fabrics.name: Elastane jersey
fabrics.note: A knit with elastane that fits the body with no darts; the cloth of swimwear, leggings and the body.

fabrics.name: Powernet
fabrics.note: A warp-knit elastic mesh for girdles, corsets and shapewear; it holds the body with no bones.

fabrics.name: Nylon sheer knit
fabrics.note: The sheer knit of the nylon stocking; on its first day of sale in 1940 women bought about four million pairs.

fabrics.name: Needle lace
fabrics.note: Lace built from buttonhole stitches with a needle; Venetian 'punto in aria' was the lace of the ruff and the collar.

fabrics.name: Bobbin lace
fabrics.note: Lace plaited from threads on many bobbins over a pattern on a pillow; Flanders and the Low Countries led it.

fabrics.name: Leavers lace
fabrics.note: Machine lace from the Leavers frame; it made lace a cloth of the middle class and of lingerie.

fabrics.name: Tulle (bobbinet)
fabrics.note: A hexagonal net from Heathcoat's bobbinet machine; the cloth of the veil, the petticoat and the tutu.

fabrics.name: Felt
fabrics.note: A cloth of matted fibres with no weave; the Pazyryk graves held felt saddle cloths and hangings. The cloth of hats.

fabrics.name: Loden
fabrics.note: A fulled and napped wool that sheds rain and wind; the coat cloth of the Alpine countries.

fabrics.name: Oilskin
fabrics.note: Cloth soaked in linseed oil for sailors and fishermen; Helly Hansen sold oiled linen in Norway from 1877.

fabrics.name: Rubberised cloth
fabrics.note: Two cotton cloths glued with naphtha-dissolved rubber; the first waterproof coat cloth, and the name of the coat.

fabrics.name: Waxed cotton
fabrics.note: A dense cotton with a paraffin-wax finish that replaced linseed oil; it does not go stiff in the cold. The cloth of the country jacket.

fabrics.name: Ventile
fabrics.note: A dense weave of long-staple cotton that swells when wet and keeps out water; made for the immersion suits of RAF pilots.

fabrics.name: Ripstop nylon
fabrics.note: A plain weave with a heavier yarn in a grid that stops a tear; made for parachutes, then shells and down jackets.

fabrics.name: Ballistic nylon
fabrics.note: A heavy basket-weave nylon made for flak jackets; it went into luggage, packs and watch straps.

fabrics.name: Nylon mesh
fabrics.note: An open warp-knit nylon that passes air and dries fast; the light upper of the running shoe, in place of leather and canvas.

fabrics.name: ePTFE membrane laminate
fabrics.note: A cloth laminated to a membrane of stretched PTFE with pores too small for water and large enough for vapour; first sold in garments in 1976.

fabrics.name: Polar fleece
fabrics.note: A napped polyester knit made with Patagonia as a light, quick-dry replacement for wool pile; sold as Polartec from 1981.

fabrics.name: Neoprene
fabrics.note: A foamed chloroprene rubber between knit faces; Hugh Bradner used it for the wetsuit in 1952, and fashion took it in the 2010s.

fabrics.name: Microfibre suede
fabrics.note: A nonwoven of very fine polyester in polyurethane that feels like suede; car cabins use it for seats and wheels.

fabrics.name: Flash-spun polyethylene
fabrics.note: A paper-like sheet of flash-spun fibre; designers use it for jackets and bags that look like envelopes.

fabrics.name: Boiled wool
fabrics.note: A wool knit that heat, water and rubbing shrink into a dense, felt-like cloth that does not fray; Tyrolean walk jackets were made of it, and Japanese designers of the 1980s used it for sculpted coats.

fabrics.name: Cashmere knit
fabrics.note: A fine knit of cashmere down, the luxury form of knitwear; the fibre came to Europe in Kashmir shawls, and plain cashmere jumpers became a sign of quiet wealth.

fabrics.name: Poly-cotton twill
fabrics.note: A dense twill of about 65 per cent polyester and 35 per cent cotton that takes a wax finish; it was made for the Nordic field jacket and trouser.

fabrics.name: Velour
fabrics.note: A soft knit with a cut pile. It covered the seats and door panels of many cars in the 1970s and 1980s.

fabrics.name: Recycled polyester knit

origin.by: Fibre made from recycled plastic bottles

fabrics.note: A knit made of polyester fibre that is spun from used plastic bottles. Car makers use it for seats and door trim.

fabrics.name: Coutil
fabrics.note: A dense cotton twill, often in a herringbone weave, that resists the pull of the bones; the standard cloth of corset bodies.

fabrics.name: Nylon tricot
fabrics.note: A fine warp-knit nylon with a smooth face and a run-resistant structure; the cloth of slips, briefs and linings.

fabrics.name: Elastic webbing
fabrics.note: A narrow woven band with rubber or elastane core threads; it forms the waistband, the strap and the leg band. Thomas Hancock patented rubber elastic for garments in 1820.

fabrics.name: Nylon webbing
fabrics.note: A narrow, tough nylon tape. A British army standard of 1973 made it the one-piece watch strap that slides under the watch.

materials.name: Vegetable-tanned leather
materials.note: Hide tanned with bark tannins; a cowhide shoe from the Areni-1 cave is about 5,500 years old. It darkens and takes a patina.

materials.name: Chrome-tanned leather
materials.note: Hide tanned with chromium salts in hours, not months; Augustus Schultz made the process commercial in 1884. Most leather now is chrome tanned.

materials.name: Calfskin
materials.note: Fine, tight-grained leather from calves for dress shoes, gloves and small leather goods.

materials.name: Shell cordovan
materials.note: Dense leather from the shell under the hide of a horse's rump; the cordwainers of Córdoba gave the trade its name.

materials.name: Suede
materials.note: Leather with the flesh side napped; the name comes from 'gants de Suède', Swedish gloves.

materials.name: Patent leather
materials.note: Leather with a hard, high-gloss lacquer; the shoe of evening dress and the 1960s boot.

materials.name: Kidskin
materials.note: Soft, thin goatskin for gloves, evening shoes and linings.

materials.name: Shearling
materials.note: Sheepskin with the wool left on; the bomber jacket, the boot and the coat lining.

materials.name: Exotic skin
materials.note: Crocodile, alligator, ostrich and lizard skin; trade in most species is under CITES control since 1975.

materials.name: Goose down
materials.note: The under-plumage of geese, in quilted baffles; Eddie Bauer patented the quilted down jacket after a near-fatal fishing trip.

materials.name: Synthetic insulation
materials.note: Fine polyester fibre batting that keeps its warmth when wet; it replaced down in wet climates.

materials.name: Natural rubber
materials.note: Latex from the rubber tree; the Olmec made rubber balls. Raw rubber goes soft in heat and hard in cold.

materials.name: Vulcanised rubber
materials.note: Rubber cured with sulphur so that it stays elastic; it made the galosh, the plimsoll and the sneaker sole.

materials.name: Crepe rubber
materials.note: Raw latex rolled into crinkled sheets for a soft, grippy sole; the sole of the desert boot and the creeper.

materials.name: EVA foam
materials.note: A light foam of ethylene-vinyl acetate for midsoles; it made the cushioned running shoe.

materials.name: PVC leathercloth
materials.note: Plasticised PVC on a knit or woven back; the upholstery of the post-war car and the cheap handbag.

materials.name: Celluloid
materials.note: The first thermoplastic, of nitrocellulose and camphor; it replaced ivory and tortoiseshell in combs, collars and frames.

materials.name: Bakelite
materials.note: The first fully synthetic plastic, a phenol-formaldehyde resin; cast Bakelite made the colourful bangles of the 1930s.

materials.name: Cellulose acetate sheet
materials.note: Plastic sheet cut and polished into eyeglass frames, with layers of colour and tortoiseshell patterns.

materials.name: Acrylic glass
materials.note: A clear, light plastic; watches used it as a crystal that does not shatter, and handbags and jewellery used it in colour.

materials.name: ABS plastic
materials.note: A tough, mouldable plastic; one-piece injection-moulded watch cases used it from 1983.

materials.name: Glass-reinforced plastic
materials.note: Glass fibre in a resin; car bodies used it from 1953 for small series with curved panels.

materials.name: Carbon fibre
materials.note: Carbon fibre in epoxy; a race car chassis used it in 1981, and watch cases and car trim use the woven look.

materials.name: Yellow gold
materials.note: Gold in carat alloys, from 9 to 22 carat; the base metal of jewellery and the dress watch case.

materials.name: Rose gold
materials.note: Gold with copper for a pink tone, called 'Russian gold' in the 19th century; it came back in the 1940s and the 2010s.

materials.name: White gold
materials.note: Gold with palladium or nickel, often plated with rhodium; a cheaper white metal than platinum after 1920.

materials.name: Platinum
materials.note: A strong white metal that holds a thin setting; jewellers used it from about 1900 for lace-like settings of diamonds.

materials.name: Sterling silver
materials.note: Silver of 925 parts in 1,000; England fixed the standard and the hallmark under Edward I in 1300.

materials.name: Pinchbeck
materials.note: A brass of copper and zinc that looks like gold; Georgian watch cases and jewellery used it.

materials.name: Brass
materials.note: Copper and zinc; buttons, buckles, eyelets, costume jewellery and car fittings.

materials.name: Stainless steel
materials.note: Steel with chromium that does not rust; the metal of the sports watch case and bracelet.

materials.name: Titanium
materials.note: A light, strong metal; the first titanium watch case came in 1970, and jewellery and eyewear followed.

materials.name: Chrome plate
materials.note: A thin bright layer of chromium on steel or brass; it made the brightwork of the car from the late 1920s.

materials.name: Aluminium

origin.by: Paul Héroult and Charles Martin Hall

materials.note: A light metal, cheap after the electrolytic process of 1886; car bodies, trunks and watch cases use it.

materials.name: Pressed steel
materials.note: Sheet steel pressed into body panels; the all-steel body replaced wood frames from the 1910s.

materials.name: Diamond
materials.note: The hardest gem; Marcel Tolkowsky set the proportions of the round brilliant cut in 1919. The first diamond trade is in India, about 400 BC.

materials.name: Coloured gemstone
materials.note: Ruby, sapphire, emerald and the semi-precious stones: amethyst, citrine, turquoise, coral, onyx and others.

materials.name: Natural pearl
materials.note: A pearl that grew in an oyster with no help; the most costly jewel of the court era.

materials.name: Cultured pearl
materials.note: A pearl grown around a nucleus that a person put in the oyster; it made the pearl necklace a jewel of the middle class.

materials.name: Paste
materials.note: Lead glass cut and foil-backed to look like diamond; Georgian paste was a jewel of its own, not only a copy.

materials.name: Jet
materials.note: A black fossil wood that polishes to a deep shine; Queen Victoria's mourning after 1861 made it the jewel of grief.

materials.name: Vitreous enamel
materials.note: Glass fused onto metal; the dial of the fine watch and the colour of Art Nouveau and Art Deco jewels.

materials.name: Synthetic sapphire
materials.note: Corundum grown by flame fusion; watch crystals use it because it scratches only under diamond.

materials.name: Technical ceramic
materials.note: Zirconium oxide sintered hard and polished; it does not scratch and does not fade, and watch cases and bracelets use it.

materials.name: Tortoiseshell
materials.note: The shell of the hawksbill turtle for combs, frames and boxes; CITES ended the trade, and acetate copies the pattern.

materials.name: Toquilla straw
materials.note: Palm-leaf straw from Ecuador, hand-woven into the 'Panama' hat.

materials.name: Burr walnut
materials.note: The figured veneer of a walnut burr; the dashboard and door cappings of the luxury car cabin.

materials.name: Feather
materials.note: Ostrich, egret and other plumes that trimmed the hat; the Victorian trade in plumes and whole birds led to the first bird-protection laws.

materials.name: Copper
materials.note: The first metal that people worked; it gave the rivet at the pocket corner of the 1873 work trouser.

materials.name: Cut steel
materials.note: Small steel studs, faceted and riveted to a plate, that catch the light like diamonds; used in jewellery from the 18th century to the 1930s.

materials.name: Horn
materials.note: Animal horn, heated and pressed or carved; it takes a translucent, amber-like colour and was a main material of Art Nouveau combs and pendants.

materials.name: Human hair
materials.note: Hair of a loved person, woven or set under glass in mourning and sentimental jewels of the 19th century. Mourning rings with hair are known from the 17th century.

materials.name: Conch shell
materials.note: The pink and white layers of the conch shell, carved as a cameo; popular in Victorian jewellery. Italian carvers cut shell cameos from the 16th century.

materials.name: Glass pearl
materials.note: A glass bead coated with a pearl-like layer; the base of the long ropes of costume jewellery. By tradition, the rosary maker Jaquin made the first one in 1656.

materials.name: Onyx
materials.note: A banded black or white chalcedony; the black onyx band gave the hard contrast of Art Deco jewellery.

materials.name: Rock crystal
materials.note: Clear quartz; it is cut, carved and engraved as a clear stone in jewels of many periods.

materials.name: Ash timber
materials.note: Pale, straight-grained hardwood that bends well after steaming. Coachbuilders and early car makers cut body frames from it.

materials.name: Nickel plate
materials.note: A thin layer of nickel on steel or brass. It gives a warm, slightly yellow shine and was the bright finish of cars before chrome.

materials.name: Polycarbonate
materials.note: A clear, tough plastic. It replaced glass in lamp lenses and became a body panel material when moulded in large parts.

materials.name: Polyurethane leatherette
materials.note: A fabric with a polyurethane skin that is embossed to look like leather. Car makers use it for seats and trim in place of hide. DuPont launched the polyurethane leather substitute Corfam in 1963.

materials.name: Whalebone (baleen)
materials.note: Plates of baleen from whales; thin strips of it stiffened stays and corsets until spring steel and plastic replaced it.

materials.name: Spring steel
materials.note: Tempered steel in thin flat strips; it gave corsets a bone that bends and returns, and it made the front busk. Steel mainsprings of clocks are known from the 15th century.

materials.name: Blued steel
materials.note: Steel heated until a thin blue oxide forms on it; watchmakers use it for screws and hands. The blue is a heat colour, not a dye.

materials.name: Gold-filled metal
materials.note: A layer of gold alloy bonded to a base metal such as brass; the layer is much thicker than gold plate. Cheap pocket watch cases used it.

materials.name: Quartz crystal
materials.note: A slice of quartz that vibrates at a fixed rate when a current passes through it. It keeps the time in a quartz clock or watch.

materials.name: Fluoroelastomer
materials.note: A soft synthetic rubber that resists sweat, oil and sunlight. Smartwatch sport bands use it. DuPont launched the fluoroelastomer Viton in 1957.

materials.name: Luminous paint
materials.note: Paint that glows in the dark. Radium salts gave the glow until the 1970s, then tritium, and from the middle 1990s strontium aluminate.

finishes.name: Indigo-dyed
finishes.note: A blue from the indigo plant; it sits on the surface of the yarn and fades with wear, the colour of denim.

finishes.name: Aniline-dyed
finishes.note: Coal-tar dyes from Perkin's mauveine; they gave the strong violets, magentas and greens of the 1860s.

finishes.name: Mercerised
finishes.note: Cotton treated with caustic soda; under tension (Horace Lowe, 1890) it takes a silk-like lustre and a deeper dye.

finishes.name: Sanforised
finishes.note: A cloth shrunk in the mill so that a garment keeps its size after a wash; it fixed the size of jeans and shirts.

finishes.name: Napped
finishes.note: Fibres raised from the surface with teasels or wire; flannel, fleece and the face of suede.

finishes.name: Fulled
finishes.note: Wool cloth beaten and wetted until the fibres mat and the cloth shrinks and thickens; loden and melton.

finishes.name: Wax-proofed
finishes.note: A paraffin or beeswax dressing that sheds water and darkens with wear; it needs a new dressing each year.

finishes.name: Water-repellent coated
finishes.note: A thin chemical finish that beads water on the face of a shell or a coat; the industry now moves to fluorine-free types.

finishes.name: Stonewashed
finishes.note: Garments tumbled with pumice for a soft hand and a pale, uneven indigo; the denim of the 1980s.

finishes.name: Block-printed
finishes.note: Colour pressed on with carved wood blocks, one block for each colour; the method of Indian calico and of the Arts and Crafts.

finishes.name: Roller-printed
finishes.note: Colour printed from engraved copper rollers at speed; it made printed cotton a cheap fashion.

finishes.name: Screen-printed
finishes.note: Colour pushed through a stencil on a mesh; the method of the printed T-shirt and the large silk-scarf design. Samuel Simon patented the method in 1907.

finishes.name: Embroidered
finishes.note: Pattern stitched into the cloth with a needle, in silk, wool, metal thread or beads.

finishes.name: Beaded and sequinned
finishes.note: Beads, sequins and paillettes sewn onto the cloth; the evening dress of the 1920s and of red-carpet couture.

finishes.name: Quilted
finishes.note: Two layers stitched through a fill in a grid of lines or channels; the down jacket and the chain-strap handbag. An ivory figure of a king in a quilted cloak is from about 3400 BC.

finishes.name: Heat-set pleated
finishes.note: Pleats fixed with heat in silk or polyester; Fortuny's Delphos gown and the pleated garments of the 1990s.

finishes.name: Glazed
finishes.note: Cloth pressed hot with starch or resin for a shine; the finish of chintz.

finishes.name: Burnished
finishes.note: Leather rubbed with wax and heat until the toe and heel go dark and glossy; the finish of the dress shoe.

finishes.name: Patent-lacquered
finishes.note: A hard lacquer at 80 GU and more; patent shoes, belts and bags. Seth Boyden made the first patent leather in 1818.

finishes.name: Distressed
finishes.note: Wear made on purpose: abrasion, rips, fades and creases.

finishes.name: Polished
finishes.note: A mirror surface at 80 GU and more on metal, gem, plastic or lacquered wood.

finishes.name: Brushed
finishes.note: Fine parallel lines from an abrasive that give a satin sheen; the case flank of a sports watch.

finishes.name: Guilloché
finishes.note: A fine engine-turned pattern cut on a rose engine. Breguet put it on watch dials from about 1786.

finishes.name: Engraved
finishes.note: Lines cut by hand with a graver; the case back of a pocket watch and the shank of a ring.

finishes.name: Enamelled
finishes.note: Glass fused into or onto metal: champlevé, cloisonné, plique-à-jour or painted.

finishes.name: Gilded
finishes.note: A thin layer of gold leaf or electroplate on base metal, leather edges or wood.

finishes.name: Rhodium-plated
finishes.note: A thin bright white layer on white gold or silver that does not tarnish.

finishes.name: PVD-coated
finishes.note: A thin hard film by physical vapour deposition, black or coloured, on steel cases and bracelets.

finishes.name: Faceted
finishes.note: Flat facets cut to return light; the round brilliant cut has 57 or 58 facets.

finishes.name: Cabochon
finishes.note: A smooth domed stone with no facets; the oldest gem cut and the crown of a Cartier watch.

finishes.name: Gloss paint
finishes.note: Body paint at 80 GU and more, solid or two-tone; the finish of the car body.

finishes.name: Metallic paint
finishes.note: Body paint with aluminium flake that sparkles in the light.

finishes.name: Matte
finishes.note: A flat surface under 10 GU: suede, raw cloth, bead-blasted metal or matte paint.

finishes.name: Woven leather
finishes.note: Thin strips of leather woven by hand into a plain weave; the 'intrecciato' of Italian leather goods.

finishes.name: Tie-dyed
finishes.note: Cloth that is tied, folded or bound before the dye bath, so that the bound parts resist the dye; Japanese shibori is an old form, and American dress took it up in the 1960s.

finishes.name: Studded
finishes.note: Metal studs or spikes fixed through cloth or leather; the biker jacket carried them, and punk dress made them a mark of the style.

finishes.name: Coated
finishes.note: A cloth or hide covered in lacquer or resin so that it sheds rain and shows a printed pattern; the grey lacquered canvas of the first flat-topped trunk is an early case.

finishes.name: Seam-taped
finishes.note: A heat-sealed strip over each needle line, so that rain cannot pass the stitch holes; the mark of a membrane shell.

finishes.name: Garment-dyed
finishes.note: A garment that is dyed after it is sewn, in a drum; it gives one colour over the cloth, the thread and the tape.

finishes.name: Foiled
finishes.note: A thin metal foil behind a stone or a paste to raise its colour and brilliance; common in Georgian jewellery.

finishes.name: Pierced
finishes.note: Openwork cut with a saw; the pierced frame lets light pass and lowers the weight of the metal.

finishes.name: Carved
finishes.note: Material cut away by hand or by tool to make a relief, a cameo or a figure.

finishes.name: Plique-a-jour
finishes.note: Enamel set in open cells with no backing, so that light passes through like stained glass.

finishes.name: Hammered
finishes.note: Metal marked with hammer blows; the dents show the hand of the maker and break the light.

finishes.name: Textured
finishes.note: A rough, deep surface made by the torch, the cast or the tool, as on rock or bark.

finishes.name: Oxidised
finishes.note: A dark film made on silver or copper by a chemical bath; it sits in the recesses and shows the relief.

finishes.name: Milgrained
finishes.note: A row of tiny beads cut along an edge of metal; it gives a fine, lace-like border.

finishes.name: Electroplated
finishes.note: A thin layer of gold, silver or chrome put on a base metal by an electric bath.

finishes.name: Anodised
finishes.note: An oxide layer grown on aluminium in an acid bath. It takes dye and gives a hard, matt, coloured surface.

finishes.name: Moulded
finishes.note: Shaped in a mould under heat or pressure, so that the part leaves the mould with its final form.
